chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 85 — The Second Dream and the First Family
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann’s 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, printed pages 61–62. The fragmentary Greek papyrus P.Oxy. XVII 2069 (fragments 1r–2r) spans 1 Enoch 85:10–86:2; its Chapter 85 overlap is limited to surviving wording in verse 10, which agrees with the sequence preserved in Geʽez. The Geʽez witness supplies the complete ten-verse chapter, including wording not preserved in the Greek fragment. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, and no text absent from the primary witnesses was supplied.

verses.text: After this I saw another dream, and I will show you the whole dream, my son.
verses.study: Enoch introduces a second vision and promises to recount it in full. Methuselah again receives revelation as a family trust meant to be preserved.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:1 — the substance of a dream is written and told
Joel 1:3 — received testimony is passed from parent to child

verses.text: Enoch raised his voice and said to his son Methuselah, ‘I will speak to you, my son. Hear my words and incline your ear to your father’s dream vision.’
verses.study: The double command to hear and incline the ear calls for active attention. The dream is not offered as entertainment but as instruction from a father to his son.
crossReferences: Proverbs 4:1 — children are called to hear a father’s instruction
Psalm 78:1 — listeners incline their ears to teaching

verses.text: ‘Before I took your mother Edna, I saw a vision on my bed. Look, a bull came out of the earth, and that bull was white. After it a heifer came out, and with her came two young bulls: one of them was black and the other red.’
verses.study: The vision retells the beginnings of the human family through cattle of different colors. The white bull and heifer stand at the head of the sequence, followed by two contrasting sons.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:7, 22 — the first man and woman begin the human family
Genesis 4:1–2 — Cain and Abel are born to the first couple

verses.text: ‘The black bull struck the red one and pursued him over the earth. From then on I could no longer see the red bull.’
verses.study: The red bull’s disappearance after the assault portrays Abel’s death without dwelling on the literal event. Violence removes a brother from sight and fractures the first family.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:8 — Cain rises against Abel and kills him
1 John 3:12 — Cain’s violence against his brother is condemned

verses.text: ‘But the black bull grew, and the heifer went with him. I saw many cattle come from him, resembling him and following after him.’
verses.study: Cain’s line increases despite the violence at its beginning. Resemblance and following suggest the transmission of a pattern across generations.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:16–24 — Cain’s descendants multiply east of Eden
Exodus 20:5–6 — the consequences of sin and the reach of covenant love extend through generations

verses.text: ‘That first heifer departed from the presence of the first bull to search for the red bull, but she did not find him. She lamented over him with a great lament and continued searching for him.’
verses.study: The mother’s searching and lament expose the human grief hidden within the animal imagery. Death brings an absence that effort cannot reverse.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:10 — Abel’s blood cries from the ground
Jeremiah 31:15 — a mother’s lament is heard for children who are no more

verses.text: ‘I watched until that first bull came to her and quieted her. From that time onward she no longer cried out.’
verses.study: The first bull shares the heifer’s grief and brings her consolation. The vision pauses its widening history to show care within the wounded household.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:4 — Adam’s family continues after the loss of Abel
2 Corinthians 1:3–4 — God’s comfort meets those who mourn

verses.text: ‘After this she bore another white bull. After him she bore many bulls and black cows.’
verses.study: The new white bull represents a renewed line after Abel’s death. The later cattle broaden the vision from one household toward the growth of humanity.
crossReferences: Genesis 4:25 — Seth is appointed as another offspring after Abel
Genesis 5:4 — other sons and daughters are born to Adam

verses.text: ‘In my sleep I saw that white bull grow in the same way and become a great white bull. From him came many white bulls, and they resembled him.’
verses.study: Seth’s symbolic line is marked by repeated whiteness and likeness. The image emphasizes continuity of character as the family expands.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:3 — Seth is born in Adam’s likeness and image
Genesis 6:9 — Noah is distinguished as righteous in his generation

verses.text: ‘They began to produce many white bulls resembling them, one following another.’
verses.study: The chapter ends with successive generations carrying forward the same symbolic likeness. This orderly line prepares for the upheaval that the vision will next reveal.
crossReferences: Genesis 5:6–29 — the line from Seth proceeds through successive generations
Luke 3:36–38 — the genealogy traces the line through Noah, Seth and Adam

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 85 begins Enoch’s second dream, often called the Animal Vision. Human beings and later nations appear as animals, allowing the vision to recount sacred history through a sustained symbolic narrative.

The opening cattle represent the first family: a white bull and heifer, then black and red young bulls. The black bull’s attack and the disappearance of the red one present Cain’s killing of Abel as the first rupture in human brotherhood.

The vision gives unusual attention to the heifer’s search and lament. Its symbolism does not make suffering abstract; it preserves the grief of a mother who cannot recover her lost son and needs consolation.

A new white bull and his white descendants signal renewed continuity through Seth’s line. Yet the multiplication of both black and white cattle also prepares the reader for a world in which family resemblance, moral direction and growing corruption will soon come into conflict.

crossReferences: Genesis 2:7, 22 — the creation of the first man and woman
Genesis 4:1–25 — Cain, Abel, violence, lament and Seth’s birth
Genesis 5:1–32 — generations from Adam through Seth to Noah
Jeremiah 31:15 — the voice of a mother’s lament
1 John 3:12 — Cain’s murder of his brother
Luke 3:36–38 — the ancestral line through Noah, Seth and Adam
